title: F1 as Organised Chaos
summary: Formula One entered the 1970s as a prestigious championship but a fragmented business. Promoters negotiated separately with teams, television coverage varied by country and event, and independent constructors depended heavily on sponsorship, start money, and prize funds. FOCA already existed, but it had not yet become the disciplined bargaining organisation it would become under Bernie Ecclestone. The mismatch between the sport's popularity and its weak collective commercial structure created the opening he exploited.

title: Bernie Ecclestone Takes Control
summary: Bernie Ecclestone bought Brabham from Ron Tauranac at the end of 1971 and became increasingly influential within the Formula One Constructors' Association. By the mid-1970s he was negotiating on behalf of the mainly British independent teams, while Max Mosley handled much of FOCA's legal and political work. Ecclestone's importance lay less in a single revelation than in bundling the teams, races, and television product into something promoters and broadcasters could buy centrally. That strategy gradually shifted power away from individual circuits and toward a permanent commercial organisation.

title: FOCA Becomes a Collective Force
summary: Under Ecclestone's leadership, FOCA became a much stronger collective representative of the constructor teams. Coordinated entry commitments and negotiations gave the teams leverage over promoters who needed a credible Formula One field, while standard contracts and pooled bargaining improved payments and predictability. The organisation did not erase conflict among teams, but it made collective withdrawal and collective negotiation plausible weapons. This commercial solidarity later became inseparable from FOCA's political struggle with FISA.

title: Television Rights Become Centralised
summary: Ecclestone progressively centralised Formula One television and promotional arrangements during the late 1970s and early 1980s. The first Concorde settlement gave FOCA a recognised role in exploiting television rights, and Ecclestone's companies later professionalised international distribution and the television presentation of races. Broadcast income grew from a secondary and inconsistent stream into a central pillar of the championship's business. Formula One was an important example of centralised sports-rights packaging, though it did not single-handedly invent the model used by every later sport.

title: The Concorde Agreement
summary: The first Concorde Agreement in 1981 ended the most destructive phase of the FISA-FOCA conflict. It confirmed the FIA/FISA's authority over sporting and technical rules, committed teams to participate, and gave FOCA a commercial role, including television exploitation. Its precise terms were confidential and later agreements repeatedly changed the balance among the governing body, teams, and Ecclestone's companies. The 100-year commercial-rights lease was a much later transaction, not a clause simply embedded in the 1981 settlement.

title: F1 Goes Global
summary: Formula One was already international before Ecclestone, but his commercial system accelerated its expansion and changed the economics of hosting. New and returning races in Australia, Hungary, Japan, Malaysia, Bahrain, China, and elsewhere broadened the calendar, often with government or promoter support. Hosting fees, television reach, sponsor markets, logistics, and political relationships all shaped the choices. The result was a championship less dependent on its traditional Western European base, but also increasingly willing to replace historic venues with higher-paying hosts.

title: The Calendar Becomes a Commercial Lever
summary: As Formula One's commercial organisation became stronger, calendar access became a valuable bargaining instrument. Promoters competed for limited dates and paid escalating fees, while the FIA formally approved the championship calendar and Ecclestone negotiated much of the commercial framework. Historic importance did not guarantee survival, and public subsidies increasingly helped new venues meet the price. Calendar control was therefore powerful but not literally Ecclestone's alone: governing-body approval, contracts, teams, broadcasters, and host governments all constrained it.

title: Manufacturers Return — and Demand More
summary: The lesson of the turbo era — that manufacturer investment could dominate Formula One — brought manufacturers back in force through the 1990s. Renault returned as an engine supplier in 1989; Mercedes partnered with Ilmor and then McLaren; BMW joined Williams; Toyota, Honda, and eventually Volkswagen Group considered full manufacturer entries. The manufacturers brought enormous resources but also demanded a larger share of the commercial revenues they believed their brand value was generating. This tension — between Ecclestone's centralised commercial control and the manufacturers' claims to a portion of the value they created — would eventually destabilise the governance structure Ecclestone had spent thirty years building.

title: Formula One Becomes a Global Media Property
summary: By the 1990s Formula One had become a highly recognisable global sports and media property, built on regular worldwide broadcasting, multinational sponsorship, and a controlled championship calendar. Its value cannot be reduced to one stable '$6 billion' figure: ownership structures, debt, rights agreements, and market conditions produced very different valuations at different moments. What was durable was the new business model—centralised rights, contractual team participation, and premium hosting fees. That model created far more revenue than the fragmented system of the early 1970s, while also concentrating decision-making power.

title: The Long Commercial-Rights Lease
summary: The FIA first granted Ecclestone-linked companies a shorter-term commercial-rights arrangement in the 1990s. In 2001, after regulatory scrutiny and internal negotiations, the FIA agreed a 100-year lease of Formula One's commercial rights beginning in 2011, reportedly for about $313.6 million. The deal sharply increased the saleable value of the Formula One business, but it remained distinct from ownership of the FIA championship itself. Its terms and the close Ecclestone-Mosley relationship have remained controversial, especially among teams that believed earlier collective rights had migrated into Ecclestone-controlled companies.

title: The War for F1's Soul
summary: The political battle that made the Concorde Agreement necessary was the FISA-FOCA War — a bitter dispute between Jean-Marie Balestre's FIA (through its sporting arm FISA) and Ecclestone's FOCA over who controlled Formula One. FISA claimed regulatory authority; FOCA claimed commercial authority. The conflict erupted into open confrontation: in 1980, the South African Grand Prix ran without FISA sanction; in 1982, the FOCA teams boycotted the San Marino Grand Prix. The manufacturers — Ferrari, Renault — backed FISA; the independent constructors backed FOCA. The war clarified what was actually at stake: not rules, but money. Ecclestone won the commercial peace by accepting Balestre's regulatory authority in exchange for control of the financial flows.

title: Private Equity Buys the Sport
summary: CVC Capital Partners assembled a controlling interest in the Formula One business during 2005–06, buying stakes held through the Bambino trust and the creditor banks that had gained control after the collapse of Kirch. Ecclestone remained chief executive and a minority stakeholder, preserving operational continuity while private equity controlled the asset. Under CVC, Formula One generated large distributions and debt-funded returns, while critics argued that too little was reinvested and that smaller teams received an inequitable share. The period demonstrated how completely the championship's commercial rights had become a financial asset separable from day-to-day racing.

title: F1 Moves Behind the Paywall
summary: Ecclestone's decision to move Formula One behind pay-television paywalls — beginning with the Sky Sports F1 channel in the UK in 2012, then Canal+ in France, then progressively across major markets — maximised short-term revenue and minimised long-term audience. The commercial logic was impeccable: Sky paid far more for exclusive rights than the BBC had paid for free-to-air coverage. The cultural consequence was severe: UK viewership fell from around 8 million per race on the BBC to under 2 million on Sky within a few years. The sport that Ecclestone had built by reaching mass television audiences was now charging those audiences for access. Critics argued it was eating its own seed corn; Ecclestone argued that the money was the point.

title: Liberty Media — A New Direction
summary: Liberty Media completed its acquisition of Formula One in January 2017 in a transaction that valued the business at roughly $8 billion including debt, with an equity value commonly reported around $4.4 billion. Ecclestone was removed from executive control and Chase Carey became chairman and chief executive. Liberty retained the long-term rights structure but invested more heavily in digital media, direct fan engagement, event presentation, and expansion in the United States. The takeover changed management style and growth strategy rather than dismantling the commercial architecture Ecclestone had built.

title: European Competition Scrutiny
summary: The European Commission investigated the FIA and Formula One's commercial arrangements in the late 1990s, focusing on conflicts between regulation and commercial exploitation and on restrictions affecting broadcasters and promoters. A 2001 settlement required clearer separation between the FIA's regulatory role and the commercial rights business, while allowing the long-term rights arrangements to proceed. The intervention did not dismantle Ecclestone's system, but it forced legal restructuring and helped define the form in which the 100-year lease operated.
